title: Reproductive Comprehensive Set 1: Pregnancy and Fetal Development (Short Answer)

questions.prompt: Where does fertilisation of the human ovum normally take place, and within what timeframe following ovulation must it occur?
questions.modelAnswer: Fertilisation normally occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube within 24 hours of ovulation.

questions.prompt: How many days after ovulation does the blastocyst typically arrive in the uterine cavity?
questions.modelAnswer: The blastocyst typically arrives in the uterine cavity 4 days after ovulation.

questions.prompt: Identify the two distinct components of the blastocyst at the time of implantation and specify which one contributes to the fetal portion of the placenta?
questions.modelAnswer: The inner mass of cells (becomes the fetus) and the trophoblast (contributes the fetal portion of the placenta).

questions.prompt: Describe the role of the syncytiotrophoblast during the implantation process.
questions.modelAnswer: The syncytiotrophoblast allows the blastocyst to penetrate deep into the endometrium by invading the maternal membranes.

questions.prompt: On which day following ovulation does implantation typically occur?
questions.modelAnswer: Implantation typically occurs 5 days after ovulation.

questions.prompt: What is the primary physiologic purpose of Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (HCG) secretion during the first trimester?
questions.modelAnswer: HCG "rescues" the corpus luteum from regression, ensuring continued production of progesterone and oestrogen to maintain the endometrium.

questions.prompt: At approximately which week of gestation do HCG levels reach their peak?
questions.modelAnswer: HCG levels peak at approximately gestational week 9.

questions.prompt: Which hormone serves as the primary indicator for chemical pregnancy tests, and how soon after ovulation can it be detected in maternal urine?
questions.modelAnswer: HCG is the indicator; it is detectable in maternal urine as early as 9 days after ovulation.

questions.prompt: Identify the primary source of oestrogen and progesterone during the first two months of pregnancy.
questions.modelAnswer: The corpus luteum.

questions.prompt: Why is the placenta considered an incomplete steroidogenic organ that must function as part of a "fetoplacental unit" to produce oestrogens?
questions.modelAnswer: The placenta lacks the enzyme 17α-hydroxylase and cannot convert progesterone to oestrogens independently; it requires androgen precursors from the fetus.

questions.prompt: Which specific oestrogen is the dominant form produced during pregnancy?
questions.modelAnswer: Estriol.

questions.prompt: Describe the metabolic pathway for estriol synthesis, starting from the fetal adrenal gland.
questions.modelAnswer: Fetal adrenal gland synthesises DHEA-S → fetal liver hydroxylates it to 16-OH DHEA-S → placenta removes sulfate and aromatises it to estriol.

questions.prompt: From where does the placenta obtain the cholesterol necessary for progesterone synthesis?
questions.modelAnswer: From the maternal circulation in the form of low-density lipoproteins (LDL).

questions.prompt: What are the primary physiologic actions of human placental lactogen (hPL), also known as human chorionic somatomammotropin (hCS), on maternal metabolism?
questions.modelAnswer: It increases lipolysis and decreases glucose utilisation in the mother to shunt nutrients toward the fetus.

questions.prompt: Describe the changes in maternal blood volume and hematocrit that typically occur during a normal pregnancy.
questions.modelAnswer: Blood volume increases significantly (by about one-third); because plasma volume increases more than red cell mass, the hematocrit falls.

questions.prompt: What effect does pregnancy have on the maternal Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR), and what is the resulting effect on serum creatinine levels?
questions.modelAnswer: GFR increases; this leads to a decrease in serum creatinine and BUN.

questions.prompt: Explain the respiratory change in maternal arterial P_(CO2)  during pregnancy and identify the hormone responsible for this change.
questions.modelAnswer: Maternal P_(CO2)decreases (hypocapnia) due to hyperventilation stimulated by progesterone.

questions.prompt: In the fetal circulation, which specific vessel carries the highest partial pressure of oxygen (P_(O2) )?
questions.modelAnswer: The umbilical vein.

questions.prompt: Define the role of the ductus venosus in the fetal circulatory pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: It bypasses the liver, directing highly oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein directly to the inferior vena cava.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the foramen ovale in the fetus, and what pressure change causes its functional closure at birth?
questions.modelAnswer: It allows blood to flow from the right atrium to the left atrium; it closes when left atrial pressure exceeds right atrial pressure after birth.

questions.prompt: Describe the purpose of the ductus arteriosus and explain why its resistance is low in utero.
questions.modelAnswer: It shunts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta to bypass the non-functional lungs; resistance is low due to the lack of oxygen in the fetal environment.

questions.prompt: Why does fetal hemoglobin (HbF) have a higher affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin (HbA)?
questions.modelAnswer: HbF does not bind 2,3-DPG as avidly as HbA, resulting in a higher affinity for O2that facilitates O2transfer from mother to fetus.

questions.prompt: Explain the term "hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction" in the context of fetal lung physiology.
questions.modelAnswer: The low P_(O2)in the fetal lungs causes vasoconstriction, increasing pulmonary vascular resistance and ensuring blood is shunted away from the lungs.

questions.prompt: What is the clinical significance of the lecithin-to-sphingomyelin (L-S) ratio measured in amniotic fluid?
questions.modelAnswer: It assesses fetal lung maturity; a ratio >2:1 indicates mature surfactant levels.

questions.prompt: Identify the three stages of normal labor and the primary events occurring in each.
questions.modelAnswer: Stage 1: Uterine contractions widen and thin the cervix; Stage 2: Fetus is delivered through the vagina; Stage 3: Placenta is delivered.
